Tiresias. The blind prophet in Greek mythology whose blindness is inseparable from his prophetic power, making him the archetype of the marginalized truth-teller no one wants to hear.

Athena blinded him. The accounts vary. Some say he saw her naked. Some say he struck her serpents. Some say he took Zeus's side in a dispute between Zeus and Hera. The exact cause matters less than the consequence: he lost his physical sight but gained something far more valuable. He received prophetic power and extreme longevity. He lived through multiple human generations, accumulating wisdom across centuries, becoming an archival witness to both divine and human history.

Tiresias appears in Sophocles's Oedipus Rex. The king summons him to reveal the truth about Oedipus's parentage and guilt. The prophet is reluctant. He knows what he knows will destroy the king. When he finally speaks, he tells the truth that Oedipus refuses to hear at first. Oedipus accuses him of being complicit in the suffering. Tiresias responds with controlled anger, speaking truth that the powerful man dismisses. This is Tiresias's story: the truth-teller whose knowledge is always accurate, yet always rejected until disaster confirms his words.

In the Odyssey, Odysseus consults him in the underworld. Tiresias speaks as a shade, a spirit from the past, and offers guidance on Odysseus's homecoming. His knowledge spans the past, the present, and the future. He is the figure who can see what mortals cannot.

The paradox at the heart of Tiresias is this: sight and blindness are inverted. True vision requires the loss of physical sight. Those with eyes to see remain blind to truth. The powerful who can see cannot access wisdom. In modern interpretations, Tiresias embodies the archetype of the outsider who sees what society refuses to acknowledge. He is valued only posthumously, only after his prophecies have proven true and it's too late to act on them.

According to some myths, Tiresias lived as both a man and a woman at different points in his life. This gave him unique insight into gender and desire. He could speak to experiences most people never have. Multiply marginalized, he stands as witness to what no one single perspective can see alone.
